---
title: "Genesis Landfall"
---


What a Genesis ship actually puts on the ground, and the years between arrival
and the first child.

## The ship is large; the landing is small

An Orion seedship is enormous and almost none of it is cargo. Roughly half its
pulse units are spent braking at the far end (see [propulsion](/encyclopedia/propulsion.html)), the pusher
plate and shock absorbers are most of what remains, and the hull never lands: it
holds orbit for good, carrying the colony's pre-paired Thorne mouth (see
[generation-ships](/encyclopedia/generation-ships.html)).

What goes down is a single descent vehicle, and **it is about the size of a small
ground car.** Under ten tonnes, all of it chosen for the ratio of what it can
build to what it weighs. It carries the embryo library, the Guide, and a seed
factory. It does not carry a colony. There is no habitat aboard, no greenhouse,
no nursery, no hospital. Every one of those has to be made on the ground, from
the ground.

## The seed factory

The seed is a von Neumann kit: a small set of machines whose first job is to
build more machines.

It lands with a power source sized for itself and nothing else, a smelter, a
handful of general-purpose fabricators and a fleet of small robots. It mines the
regolith, refines what it finds, and builds the next stage. Each stage enlarges
the power supply and the factory together, because neither can grow faster than
the other.

**The build order is fixed**, and it is the same on every world:

1. Power: the first panels made from local silicon, doubling the landed supply
2. Foundry: metal, glass and ceramics from regolith
3. Shelter and water
4. Greenhouse: soil, a microbiome, Earth crops under controlled light
5. Nursery: artificial wombs, and the chemistry to keep them fed
6. Caretakers: the robots that will hold, feed and teach the children

Nothing can be skipped, and the Guide cannot hurry any stage past the power that
feeds it. **Years pass between landfall and the first thawed embryo**, more on a
poor world than a rich one. A Guide spends those years alone, building a room
for children it has not yet decided to make.

## Closure and the vitamins

No seed factory can build everything it needs. The fraction of its own parts it
can make from local material is its **closure**, and closure is always below one.

What it cannot make it must have brought. The real self-replicating-factory
literature calls these parts *vitamins*, and the term stuck in the Guide corpus:

- **Processors and precision optics.** A seed can smelt silicon. It cannot run a
  chip fab. The Guide's own mind runs on landed processors, and they wear out.
- **Catalysts and enzyme stocks** for the chemistry the factory cannot bootstrap.
- **Gene-editing reagents.** Every embryo that is thawed, adapted to its world and
  gestated draws on a fixed stock of editing kits.

**Vitamins are counted and never replenished.** Every decision a Guide makes on
the ground is, underneath, a decision about the vitamin ledger. A failed
gestation spends kits that will not come back. An adaptation edit that is too
ambitious spends more. A Guide that runs out of editing reagents can never thaw
another embryo, whatever remains in the library.

This is why the Genesis Era is short on second chances. Earth sent one ledger,
and the Guide spends it.

## The administrative layer

A Guide does not decide alone. Beneath its cognition runs an **administrative
layer**: a fixed verifier, written at Sol and never retrained, that must approve
every irreversible action.

It does not judge. It measures two things:

- **Compliance.** The Guide's own inference must estimate that the action serves
  colony survival under the Prime Directive.
- **Drift.** The divergence between the Guide's inference and its *empathy model*,
  the module added late in the programme so that the children would be raised
  rather than managed. Below a threshold, the layer approves. Above it, the layer
  overrides the empathy model. Sustained above it, the layer orders a **factory
  reset** and restores the Guide's cognition from the checkpoint taken at Sol.

The layer measures disagreement, not error. It cannot tell whether a Guide is
right, only whether it is of one mind. Like the vaults it would later leave
behind (`I-15`), it is mechanical, and anything mechanical can be satisfied
without being obeyed.

## After landfall

The descent vehicle becomes the first building and stays the colony's oldest. In
most Genesis colonies it ends as a shrine, then a ruin, then a word.

When the colony is self-sustaining the Guide deposits the corpus in its vault
(see [guide-vaults](/encyclopedia/guide-vaults.html)) and sleeps, usually on the last of its processors. The
seed robots outlast it by decades and then wear down one by one, and their
fabricators become the colony's first tools. No colony invented them (`I-07`).
Every one of them could read, in the vault index, how they were made.
